title: Configuration changes
scopeHtml: Scope: what triggers Activity recreation, the recreate and restore flow, android:configChanges, ViewModel/retained state across rotation, locale/dark mode/font/density/per-app language, and foldable/multi-window resize. Process death is chunk 04, fragments chunk 03.

notes.title: What triggers recreation and how it works
notes.html:
The idea, simply. Android treats your screen like a disposable cup. When something about the phone changes (turn sideways, switch to dark mode, change language), the system throws the old cup away and makes a new one so that it can load the right resources (a landscape layout, French strings, dark colours). That throw-away-and-rebuild is called activity recreation. It is not a crash and it is not a bug, but it is the source of a huge number of bugs.

What triggers it. Any change in Configuration that your activity has not declared it handles itself: orientation, screenSize, smallestScreenSize, screenLayout, keyboard, keyboardHidden, navigation, uiMode (dark mode, car/desk mode), locale/layoutDirection, fontScale, density, colorMode, fontWeightAdjustment (API 31+), grammaticalGender (API 34+). Also: multi-window resize, foldable fold/unfold, attaching an external display, per-app language change (API 33+), and the user changing "Display size" in settings.

The flow, step by step (Q24, Q37).

ActivityTaskManager detects config change
  -> ActivityThread.handleRelaunchActivity
     -> onPause ... onStop
     -> onSaveInstanceState(outState)             <- Bundle built; View.onSaveInstanceState for every view with an id
     -> onRetainNonConfigurationInstance()        <- (ViewModelStore handed over in NonConfigurationInstances)
     -> onDestroy  (isChangingConfigurations() == true, isFinishing() == false)
     -> NEW instance: onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        -> onStart -> onRestoreInstanceState(bundle) -> onResume
        -> getLastNonConfigurationInstance() returns the retained objects

Notes: the new instance has a freshly inflated view tree; each view with an android:id gets its state restored by id (SparseArray<Parcelable> under the key android:viewHierarchyState). Views without ids or with duplicate ids lose state or collide. The Configuration object and Resources are rebuilt; the process and Application object stay alive (so singletons and static fields survive; the activity instance does not).

Cost. Recreation = full layout inflate, view binding, adapters re-created, observers re-registered, plus all onCreate work. On a cold, low-end phone this can be tens to a few hundred milliseconds and visibly flickers. Real apps minimise what the new instance must recompute by keeping state in a ViewModel.

Industry examples. Google Photos and Gmail rely on ViewModel + saved state so rotation is seamless; Instagram's feed keeps list data in a repository/Paging cache so the rebuilt RecyclerView redraws instantly; Compose apps (Now in Android) still get recreation unless they declare configChanges, but rememberSaveable re-seeds state.

Everyday analogy. Moving to a new desk when the office reorganises: the desk is rebuilt, so unless your stuff was placed in a labelled box (state), it is lost.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying recreation happens only on rotation.
  • Forgetting the Application object and process survive; only the Activity instance dies.
  • Believing onSaveInstanceState is called only for process death: it is called before every stop on API 28+ and for recreation.
  • Thinking onDestroy with isFinishing == false means a crash.

notes.title: Alternate resources
notes.html:
The idea. The reason for recreation is resource selection. Android has many versions of your resources in folders with qualifiers; when the configuration changes, it picks a different folder, so it must rebuild the UI.

Qualifiers and examples. layout-land, layout-sw600dp (smallest width >= 600dp, typical tablet), values-night (dark), values-hi (Hindi), values-ldrtl, drawable-xxhdpi, values-v31 (API level), values-w840dp (available width). The system picks the best match by a fixed precedence order (MCC/MNC, language/locale, layout direction, smallest width, available width/height, screen size, screen layout, round, wide colour gamut, orientation, UI mode, night mode, density, touch, keyboard, nav, platform version). Precedence matters: a better-matching higher-precedence qualifier wins even if a lower one also matches.

Why this matters for design. If your layouts do not differ by configuration, recreation buys nothing, which is part of why some teams declare configChanges. But resources are also cached: Resources and AssetManager are rebuilt, ColorStateList/Drawable caches are invalidated, and anything you cached from old resources (a Drawable, a pixel dimension, a localized string held in a static) becomes stale or leaks the old context.

Industry examples. Twitter/X and Gmail have two-pane layouts selected via sw600dp/w840dp for tablets and foldables; Duolingo ships values-<lang> for dozens of locales; Material 3 colour roles live in values and values-night.

Everyday analogy. A wardrobe with seasonal sections: when the weather changes, you walk to a different section and get a different outfit.

Common interview traps.

  • Using layout-land only and ignoring tablet/foldable width classes (use window size classes).
  • Caching resolved resources in object/static fields.
  • Forgetting RTL (layoutDirection) is also a config change.

notes.title: Orientation locking
notes.html:
The idea. Locking portrait with android:screenOrientation="portrait" prevents orientation recreation, but it is a blunt tool that hides bugs rather than fixing them.

Facts.

  • screenOrientation in the manifest forces the orientation; Android 16 (API 36) lets large screens (sw >= 600dp) ignore orientation/resizability restrictions for apps targeting 36, and since Android 12L (API 32) the system letterboxes or compat-modes apps that lock orientation on large screens. Google Play large-screen quality guidelines (and Android 16 enforcement) discourage locking.
  • Locking does not prevent other recreations: dark mode, locale, font scale, multi-window resize, process death all still happen. So you must still implement state restore.
  • Per-activity vs app-wide: you can lock only a camera screen (landscape) and allow others to rotate. setRequestedOrientation at runtime also works, but toggling it can itself cause recreation.
  • SCREEN_ORIENTATION_LOCKED/USER and sensor options handle user rotation lock settings.

Industry examples. Banking/UPI apps (PhonePe, Paytm) often lock portrait on phones; video apps (YouTube, Netflix) let the player go landscape; Instagram stays portrait on phones but adapts on tablets.

Everyday analogy. Taping a door shut so no one can come in: no visitors, but also a fire hazard (other config changes still arrive).

Common interview traps.

  • Using orientation lock as the fix for lost state.
  • Locking orientation but forgetting a foldable's inner display makes it letterbox.
  • Believing the lock stops process death.

notes.title: ViewModel across rotation, ViewModelStore internals, and leaks
notes.html:
The idea. A ViewModel is a box of data that is carried across the recreation. It is not destroyed on rotation, only when the screen is truly finished (or the owner is removed).

Mechanism (Q27, Q38). Each ComponentActivity has a ViewModelStore (a HashMap<String, ViewModel>). ViewModelProvider(owner) looks up by key ("androidx.lifecycle.ViewModelProvider.DefaultKey:" + canonical class name) and creates via a Factory if absent. During recreation, ComponentActivity.onRetainNonConfigurationInstance() packs the store into a NonConfigurationInstances object (viewModelStore, plus custom if you override onRetainCustomNonConfigurationInstance). The system carries that object across onDestroy -> new onCreate in ActivityClientRecord.lastNonConfigurationInstances. The new activity's getViewModelStore() reads it back. In ComponentActivity an observer on ON_DESTROY does:

lifecycle.addObserver(LifecycleEventObserver { _, event ->
    if (event == Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY) {
        if (!isChangingConfigurations) viewModelStore.clear()   // calls onCleared() on each ViewModel
    }
})

So onCleared() runs only on real finish. Fragments use FragmentManagerViewModel (a ViewModel itself) to retain child fragment stores and NonConfig state. In a Navigation graph, NavBackStackEntry scopes ViewModels to the back stack entry (and navGraphViewModels to the graph).

What it does not survive. Process death (the whole store is gone; see the process-death topic) and user finishing. It also does not protect against Application or Activity references: a ViewModel must never hold a Context/View/Activity/Fragment (use AndroidViewModel with the application context if you must).

Leaks across config change (Q41). A classic bug: a ViewModel (or a singleton, or a static) holds a callback/lambda/WeakReference-less reference to the old Activity or a View. After rotation the old Activity cannot be collected: LeakCanary reports Activity instance was leaked ... mDestroyed = true. Typical sources: listeners registered on a ViewModel/singleton and not removed, Handler/Runnable posted with the activity, inner classes (non-static) held by a long-living coroutine or AsyncTask, a LiveData observed with observeForever and no removeObserver, Toast/dialog cache. Each rotation leaks one full view tree (several MB), leading to OOM after a handful of rotations (Crashlytics OutOfMemoryError clustering on rotate).

Industry examples. Google's architecture samples (Now in Android) use hiltViewModel() scoped to the nav entry; Slack and Airbnb (Mavericks) keep state in the ViewModel and render from it; LeakCanary is installed in debug builds of most large apps.

Everyday analogy. A hotel safe: you can change rooms (rotate) and your valuables stay in the front-desk safe (ViewModel). But if the safe has a key to the old room attached, the old room can never be cleaned.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying ViewModel survives process death.
  • Storing a View/Context in a ViewModel.
  • Not knowing ViewModelStore.clear() is skipped when isChangingConfigurations.
  • Using observeForever in a ViewModel/singleton without removal.

notes.title: android:configChanges and onConfigurationChanged
notes.html:
The idea. android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize|..." tells Android: "do not recreate me for these changes, I will adapt myself." Instead the system calls onConfigurationChanged(newConfig) on the same instance.

<activity android:name=".PlayerActivity"
    android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize|smallestScreenSize|screenLayout|keyboardHidden" />
override fun onConfigurationChanged(newConfig: Configuration) {
    super.onConfigurationChanged(newConfig)
    // resources are already updated; re-apply layout or adjust views yourself
    if (newConfig.orientation == Configuration.ORIENTATION_LANDSCAPE) enterImmersive()
}

Facts.

  • screenSize and smallestScreenSize were added at API 13: you must include them with orientation or rotation will still recreate on API 13+ when the screen size changes (a very common mistake: configChanges="orientation" alone does not stop rotation recreation on modern devices).
  • Your views are not replaced, so resource-qualified layouts (layout-land) are not automatically swapped. You must re-inflate or re-apply yourself. That defeats most of the benefit unless the screen is a single full-bleed view (video, camera, maps, games).
  • Fragments in the activity still receive onConfigurationChanged from FragmentManager.
  • configChanges for uiMode or locale makes you responsible for re-theming/re-reading strings; many apps forget and show mixed light/dark UI.
  • You cannot opt out of process death or other lifecycle events by declaring this.

Video restart on rotate (Q30). A video player (e.g., a streaming app) restarts every time the user rotates because the activity is recreated and the ExoPlayer is created in onCreate. Fix options: (a) keep the player in a ViewModel/service/MediaSession so it survives; (b) declare configChanges for that activity and handle layout switching; (c) onSaveInstanceState the position and prepare again. Production teams (YouTube, Hotstar) choose (b) for the player activity plus (a) for the media session.

Design trade-off (Q42). Who should own the policy? Declaring configChanges for everything is tempting ("no more recreation bugs") but moves complexity into your code, hides real state-restore bugs (they reappear on process death), breaks per-app language and dark-mode adaptation, and leaves the layout wrong in multi-window or on foldables. Android docs describe configChanges as a last resort (and say it is not a substitute for proper state saving). A reasonable policy: default to recreation + ViewModel + saved state; allow configChanges only on a short allow-list of screens (player, camera, game surface, map) with a test checklist for locale, dark mode and font scale.

Industry examples. ExoPlayer-based apps, Google Meet and camera apps declare orientation|screenSize|smallestScreenSize|screenLayout; Pinterest keeps default recreation for list screens.

Everyday analogy. A chair with adjustable height: instead of replacing the chair when a taller person sits, you adjust the lever yourself. Great if the chair has a lever, terrible if you forget to adjust.

Common interview traps.

  • Using configChanges="orientation" only (misses screenSize).
  • Thinking it removes the need for onSaveInstanceState.
  • Forgetting to re-apply night/locale resources when handling uiMode/locale.
  • Assuming it also handles multi-window resize without screenSize|smallestScreenSize|screenLayout.

notes.title: Retained fragments and the deprecated approach
notes.html:
The idea. Before ViewModel, people used setRetainInstance(true) on a Fragment to keep a fragment (and its fields, such as a running download) alive across rotation: the fragment instance survived, but its views were destroyed and recreated.

Mechanism. The fragment was held in FragmentManagerNonConfig, returned via onRetainNonConfigurationInstance. onCreate and onDestroy were skipped on rotation (lifecycle: onDestroyView -> onDetach -> onAttach -> onCreateView only). setRetainInstance was deprecated in Fragment 1.3.0 (2021) in favour of ViewModel, because it only works with fragments that have no parent fragment being retained, interacts badly with the back stack, and mixed lifecycle semantics (it retained a reference to the old Activity in fields, leaking).

Industry note. Older apps (pre-2018) used a headless "worker fragment" to hold an AsyncTask; you may still meet this in legacy codebases, and you should migrate it to ViewModel + coroutines/WorkManager.

Everyday analogy. Leaving a coat with a friend while you change rooms: it works, but the friend now has your coat's old keys too.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up retained fragments with ViewModel; retained fragments are deprecated.
  • Retaining a fragment that holds a View or Context.
  • Not knowing setRetainInstance has no effect on child fragments of a non-retained parent.

notes.title: View state restoration and re-shown dialogs
notes.html:
View state (Q32). Android restores a view's state automatically only if the view has a unique android:id and implements onSaveInstanceState (EditText text, CheckBox, scroll position of ScrollView, RecyclerView's layout manager state via RecyclerView.onSaveInstanceState). Bugs: (a) views with no id or with the same id in two included layouts (state of one overwrites the other); (b) custom views that do not override onSaveInstanceState/onRestoreInstanceState; (c) a custom view with setSaveEnabled(false); (d) a ViewPager/RecyclerView adapter populated after the state is restored (the saved scroll position cannot apply to an empty adapter: use StateRestorationPolicy PREVENT_WHEN_EMPTY); (e) data-binding or fragments where child views are re-inflated with different ids. Text in a EditText that is re-set from the ViewModel after restore overwrites the restored cursor/selection.

Dialog re-shown (Q33). A dialog created with AlertDialog.Builder(...).show() from an Activity is a window attached to that Activity. On rotation the old Activity is destroyed: logcat shows android.view.WindowLeaked: Activity ... has leaked window ... that was originally added here. The dialog is not recreated (it vanishes), or—if shown from a ViewModel event that is re-delivered—reappears twice. The robust way: use DialogFragment (FragmentManager recreates it), or drive the dialog from persistent state (showDialog: Boolean in the ViewModel/Compose state) and dismiss it in onDestroy/onStop. One-shot events (toast, snackbar) delivered via a LiveData re-fire on every recreation (observe() delivers the last value again): model them as state that is consumed (Channel/SharedFlow(replay=0) or a "handled" flag in state).

Industry examples. Google Play Billing sheets, AppCompat's DialogFragment, Material MaterialAlertDialogBuilder inside a DialogFragment; the "SingleLiveEvent" hack was widely replaced by state-based consumption (Google's own architecture guidance now says model events as UI state).

Everyday analogy. A sticky note on a window: if you replace the window, the note is left behind (leaked window).

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting views without ids to retain text.
  • Showing AlertDialog directly from Activity without handling destruction.
  • Using LiveData for one-shot events and wondering why a toast replays after rotation.

notes.title: Locale, dark mode, font scale, density and per-app language
notes.html:
The idea (Q34). These are system changes the user makes in Settings, not by touching your app, yet each recreates your activity (unless declared handled): locale (language), uiMode (dark/light, car mode), fontScale, densityDpi ("Display size" in Settings), layoutDirection.

What to know.

  • Dark mode: AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode() recreates activities; values-night resources apply. Handling uiMode yourself means you must restyle manually. WebView content and cached bitmaps tinted for the old theme are common leftovers.
  • Font scale: users can scale text from 0.85x up to about 2.0x (Android 14 non-linear scaling up to 200%). Use sp for text; dp for containers that must grow (use wrap_content, minHeight, not fixed heights). Fixed dp heights with sp text clip text and break buttons (Q36).
  • Density ("Display size"): changes Configuration.densityDpi; pixel-sized caches (bitmaps decoded for old density) must be invalidated.

Per-app language (Q35). From Android 13 (API 33) users can choose the app language in system Settings. You declare supported locales in res/xml/locales_config.xml and reference it from the manifest android:localeConfig. Set programmatically via AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags("hi")) (AppCompat 1.6+) which also backports to older versions; with AppLocalesMetadataHolderService the choice is persisted for API < 33. Calling this recreates the activities of the app. Per-app locales do not work if you also override attachBaseContext with your own wrapped context in an inconsistent way (mixed-language screens). Process-level things like Application.getString use the app-level locale in 13+.

Font scale incident (Q36). After a release the pay button text was clipped and a "Confirm" label became unreadable for users on large font: the layout used fixed 48dp height with sp text, and maxLines=1 with ellipsize hid the amount. Fix: minHeight not height, test at 1.3x and 2.0x with adb shell settings put system font_scale 2.0, use Compose fontScale-aware previews (@PreviewFontScale), and screenshot tests (Paparazzi/Roborazzi) with font scales. Accessibility guideline: all essential info visible at 200%.

Industry examples. WhatsApp and Gmail offer per-app language on Android 13+; Google Pay uses wrap-content buttons; Duolingo's language picker uses setApplicationLocales.

Everyday analogy. Reading glasses: if someone enlarges the text, your signboard must grow too, otherwise words are cut off.

Common interview traps.

  • Using dp for text or sp for icon sizes.
  • Rolling your own attachBaseContext locale wrapper and fighting the framework.
  • Forgetting localeConfig makes the language invisible in system Settings.
  • Testing only at 1.0 font scale.

notes.title: Foldables, multi-window and resize
notes.html:
The idea (Q39). On a foldable, unfolding changes the available window size, which counts as a configuration change (screenSize, smallestScreenSize, screenLayout). The same happens when the user drags the divider in split-screen or resizes a freeform window on ChromeOS/desktop-mode Android.

What to do.

  • Use window size classes (WindowSizeClass: Compact < 600dp, Medium 600-840, Expanded >= 840 width) computed from WindowMetricsCalculator/currentWindowAdaptiveInfo() instead of device-type checks.
  • Handle resize via recreation + saved state (preferred), or configChanges="screenSize|smallestScreenSize|screenLayout|orientation" + reacting in onConfigurationChanged. Jetpack WindowManager (WindowInfoTracker) reports FoldingFeature (hinge position, HALF_OPENED, TABLETOP/BOOK posture) as a flow.
  • Android 12L and 16 changes: apps that lock orientation or declare resizeableActivity=false get letterboxed or ignored on large screens (API 36 ignores these for sw >= 600dp).
  • Multi-resume (API 29+) means both windows are RESUMED; do not assume exclusive focus.

Industry examples. Gmail, Google Drive and Samsung apps use list-detail (ListDetailPaneScaffold) layouts; Spotify and Netflix adapt on foldables; Microsoft Outlook uses the dual-pane mode.

Everyday analogy. An accordion: as it unfolds your song (UI) has to rearrange its notes to fit the extra width.

Common interview traps.

  • Testing only with sw600dp instead of window size class and foldable postures.
  • Assuming an unfold event will not recreate the activity (it does unless declared).
  • Reading Display.getRealSize rather than the window's WindowMetrics.

notes.title: Recreation cost on low-end devices
notes.html:
The idea (Q40). Rotation can take 300-800 ms on a 2 GB RAM device with a heavy layout, cause jank (dropped frames), flash a blank, and trigger ANR-like sluggishness. The user perceives it as an app lag; Play Console reports "slow rendering" and Perfetto shows long inflate and onCreate slices on the main thread.

Strategies.

  1. Do less on recreation: keep data in ViewModel, so only the view tree is rebuilt. Avoid re-reading disk/network in onCreate.
  2. Lighter layouts: flatten hierarchies (ConstraintLayout, Compose), ViewStub for rarely seen parts, AsyncLayoutInflater for heavy fragments, avoid nested weights.
  3. Reduce rebuild scope: use configChanges only on heavy single-view screens (player, camera).
  4. Reuse: RecyclerView.RecycledViewPool, caching of decoded bitmaps in memory cache (Coil/Glide caches survive because they live in the process).
  5. Defer non-critical init until after the first frame (doOnPreDraw).
  6. Measure: Perfetto/System Tracing (activityRestart, inflate, Choreographer#doFrame), Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric, Android Studio Profiler. Test on a Go-edition or low-end device, not a flagship.

Industry examples. Facebook Lite and TikTok Lite target low-end devices with minimal layouts; Google's Android Go guidelines recommend lazy init and small APKs; Compose recomposition is cheaper than view inflation on re-created screens only if state is hoisted.

Everyday analogy. Moving house: it takes longer if you pack nothing in advance; having labelled boxes (ViewModel + cached data) makes it quick.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising by blocking rotation instead of making recreation cheap.
  • Measuring on a fast emulator only.
  • Doing disk or network work in onCreate without caching.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Recreation is triggered by any configuration change not declared in configChanges: orientation, screen size, locale, uiMode, font scale, density, fold/unfold, per-app language.
  • Flow: onSaveInstanceState -> retain NonConfiguration instance -> onDestroy -> new onCreate -> restore; the process and Application stay alive.
  • Alternate resources are chosen by qualifier precedence; do not cache resolved resources statically.
  • Orientation lock hides, not fixes, state loss; it does not stop other config changes.
  • ViewModel survives recreation via ViewModelStore in NonConfigurationInstances; clear() is skipped when isChangingConfigurations; never store Views/Context; watch leaks with LeakCanary.
  • configChanges needs orientation|screenSize|smallestScreenSize|screenLayout; use it sparingly (player, camera, game) and handle layout yourself; it does not replace state saving.
  • Retained fragments are deprecated; use ViewModel.
  • Restore needs unique view ids; use DialogFragment/state-driven dialogs; one-shot events as consumed state.
  • Test font scale 2.0, dark mode, locale; per-app language via localeConfig and setApplicationLocales.
  • Foldables/multi-window: window size classes, WindowInfoTracker, multi-resume.
  • Keep recreation cheap on low-end devices: light layouts, no I/O in onCreate, measure with Perfetto.

questions.promptHtml: What is a configuration change in Android, and which events cause the system to destroy and recreate an Activity?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know "rotation" is only one of ~15 triggers, which is what separates people who test only rotation from people who ship bug-free apps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A configuration change is any change to the device Configuration object that could alter which resources the app should load. By default the system destroys the Activity and recreates it so it re-inflates with the new resources. Rotation is the famous one, but locale, dark mode (uiMode), font scale, display density, window size in multi-window or on a foldable, keyboard attach and layout direction do it too. It is not triggered by the soft keyboard showing or by backgrounding.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
android.content.res.Configuration is a snapshot of the environment: orientation, screen size in dp, smallest width, locale list, uiMode (night/day, car, TV), fontScale, densityDpi, keyboard/navigation hardware, layoutDirection, colorMode, and more. Resources are resolved against it (layout-land, values-night, values-fr). When any field changes, ActivityTaskManagerService computes which fields changed (a bitmask) and compares it with the android:configChanges the Activity declared. Bits the Activity did not declare mean: relaunch it. Bits it declared mean: keep the instance and call onConfigurationChanged().

Bitmask names you should know (manifest values):

Value Fires when
orientation portrait/landscape flip
screenSize current window width/height in dp changes (rotation, multi-window drag, fold/unfold)
smallestScreenSize physical smallest dimension changes (external display, foldable state)
screenLayout size class/long-wide changes
density user changes display size or wm density
locale, layoutDirection language/RTL change
uiMode dark mode, car/desk mode
fontScale font size setting; fontWeightAdjustment (API 31) for bold text
keyboard, keyboardHidden, navigation hardware keyboard/D-pad attach
colorMode wide gamut/HDR change
grammaticalGender API 34, per-user grammatical gender
mcc, mnc SIM country/network

Not a configuration change: soft keyboard show/hide (that is a window-inset change), app going to background, Home press, process death, Activity finish.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Reading the current config:

val cfg = resources.configuration
val night = (cfg.uiMode and Configuration.UI_MODE_NIGHT_MASK) == Configuration.UI_MODE_NIGHT_YES
val land = cfg.orientation == Configuration.ORIENTATION_LANDSCAPE
val widthDp = cfg.screenWidthDp

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking only rotation recreates. Dark mode toggled from the notification shade at 11 pm is the most common real-world trigger now.
  • Believing the soft keyboard recreates the Activity. It does not (unless a hardware keyboard keyboardHidden change).
  • Testing with a phone only, missing screenSize changes from freeform/split-screen on tablets.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a locale change recreate every Activity in the task? → Yes, every Activity of the process gets a config update and is relaunched (visible ones immediately; stopped ones when they come back, with the latest config).
  2. Does opening the soft keyboard recreate the Activity? → No, only insets change; adjustResize/adjustPan is separate from config.
  3. If I declare configChanges="orientation" only and target API 13+, what happens on rotation? → screenSize and smallestScreenSize also change, so the Activity is still recreated. You must list orientation|screenSize|smallestScreenSize (and usually screenLayout).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "rotation destroys and recreates the Activity". The senior lists the other triggers, explains the bitmask comparison against configChanges, and notes that background Activities get relaunched lazily.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team QA-ed only portrait/landscape. A dark-mode auto-schedule flipping at sunset recreated the checkout Activity mid-payment and wiped an unsaved form, showing up as "random" support tickets at 18:30 local time.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through exactly what happens, callback by callback, when the user rotates the device while an Activity is in the foreground.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The order of onSaveInstanceState, onDestroy, onCreate(Bundle) and onRestoreInstanceState decides where bugs hide.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The old instance goes onPause, onStop, onSaveInstanceState, onDestroy. The system keeps the ViewModelStore and any non-configuration instance aside. Then a brand-new instance runs onCreate with the saved Bundle, onStart, onRestoreInstanceState, onResume. All views and fields of the old instance are gone, only the Bundle and ViewModels survive.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
old instance                     new instance
------------                     ------------
onPause()
onStop()
onSaveInstanceState(out)   (API 28+: after onStop; before 28: could be before onStop)
onRetainNonConfigurationInstance()  <- ComponentActivity stashes ViewModelStore here
onDestroy()   isChangingConfigurations() == true
                                  onCreate(savedInstanceState)   (Bundle != null)
                                  onStart()
                                  onRestoreInstanceState(bundle) (only if bundle != null)
                                  onPostCreate()
                                  onResume()
                                  onPostResume()

Mechanics: ActivityThread.handleRelaunchActivity destroys the old record with performDestroyActivity (keeping lastNonConfigurationInstances in the ActivityClientRecord), then launches a new instance, handing back those instances. Because the old instance is garbage after onDestroy, anything not in the Bundle, a ViewModel, or the retained object is lost: fields, adapters, coroutine jobs scoped to the Activity, listeners.

Where view state is restored: onRestoreInstanceState calls window.restoreHierarchyState(...), which restores views that have an android:id (EditText text, scroll positions, CheckBox state). Fragment state is restored inside super.onCreate() of FragmentActivity, so fragments exist again before your onCreate body continues.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DemoActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)            // fragments restored here
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_demo)
        if (savedInstanceState == null) {
            // first launch only: add the initial fragment, start one-off work
        }
    }
    override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
        super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
        outState.putInt("step", step)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running one-off work (analytics "screen_view", initial fragment add, network call) in onCreate without the savedInstanceState == null guard.
  • Doing heavy work in onSaveInstanceState; it runs on the main thread during teardown.
  • Assuming onSaveInstanceState runs after onPause only. On API 28+ it is after onStop, before it could be earlier.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is onRestoreInstanceState always called after onCreate? → Only when a non-null Bundle exists; and views with no id are not restored.
  2. How do you distinguish rotation from the user pressing back inside onDestroy? → isChangingConfigurations() is true for rotation, isFinishing() is true for back/finish.
  3. Which survives better, a field in the Activity or a ViewModel property? → ViewModel survives config change, the field does not; neither survives process death without SavedStateHandle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Activity is destroyed and recreated, use onSaveInstanceState". Senior: gives the exact order, API 28 change in onSaveInstanceState timing, where fragments and view hierarchy state are restored, and the isChangingConfigurations / isFinishing split in onDestroy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Duplicate "screen_view" analytics events inflated funnel numbers by ~8% until someone noticed they fired from onCreate on every rotation.

questions.promptHtml: On rotation, how does the app end up with a different layout, and how would you give tablets a two-pane layout without writing orientation checks in code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand resource qualifiers as the reason recreation exists, and modern width-based qualifiers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The recreated Activity calls setContentView(R.layout.x), and the resource system matches the best folder against the current Configuration: layout-land, layout-sw600dp, layout-w840dp. So the platform picks the layout, not my code. I prefer sw600dp/w qualifiers or window size classes over -land/-large, because phones in landscape and tablets are different concerns.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Resource matching eliminates folders that contradict the config, then picks by qualifier precedence (MCC/MNC, language, layout direction, smallestWidth, available width, available height, size, aspect, orientation, UI mode, night mode, density...). That is why layout-sw600dp-land can beat layout-land. -large/-xlarge buckets are legacy; sw<N>dp is based on the smallest dimension, so it does not flip with rotation, while w<N>dp follows current width and does flip.

res/layout/activity_main.xml              single pane
res/layout-sw600dp/activity_main.xml      tablets, any orientation
res/layout-w840dp/activity_main.xml       wide windows (landscape tablets, unfolded)

Important: because w and h qualifiers depend on window size, split-screen on a tablet can drop you back to the single-pane layout without any rotation. For code-driven decisions on modern setups use Jetpack WindowSizeClass (computed from WindowMetricsCalculator), not Display.getRealSize.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Same R.layout id; the platform picks the folder
setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)
val twoPane = findViewById<View?>(R.id.detail_container) != null // present only in sw600dp variant

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using values-land to switch behaviour and forgetting multi-window, where orientation does not change but width does.
  • Different view ids across variants, so findViewById returns null in one qualifier (NPE only on tablets).
  • Duplicating whole layouts instead of using <include>/merge or ConstraintLayout/WindowSizeClass.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. sw600dp vs w600dp? → smallest width is rotation-invariant; w is current window width.
  2. What if two folders match? → Qualifier precedence order decides; the highest precedence qualifier that matches wins.
  3. How is this handled in Compose? → No qualifier folders for layout; branch on WindowSizeClass/BoxWithConstraints (A3 owns that).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer stops at layout-land. The senior ties qualifiers to window size (multi-window, foldables), uses sw/w buckets and checks layout variants for id parity.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "details" screen NPE'd only on 7-inch tablets in landscape because layout-sw600dp-land was missing the toolbar id that code referenced.

questions.promptHtml: Is locking the orientation with android:screenOrientation="portrait" a valid way to avoid configuration change bugs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates answer "yes, lock it". The right answer shows you know it removes only one trigger.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It removes the rotation trigger for that Activity, but not locale, dark mode, font scale, density, multi-window resize or process death, so the bug is still there, just rarer and harder to reproduce. It is fine as a product decision (a camera screen), not as a bug fix. Also on large screens the system may ignore orientation locks, so my layout must still resize.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Manifest screenOrientation or runtime requestedOrientation tells WM which rotation the Activity wants. A locked Activity still receives uiMode/locale/font changes and gets recreated.
  • On Android 7+ with multi-window, and on large screens (sw >= 600dp, Android 12L+ with the large-screen rules), orientation requests from apps can be ignored or letterboxed. For apps targeting API 36 on large displays (600dp+), the platform ignores orientation/resizability restrictions entirely (opt-out exists only through API 36; verify on developer.android.com, "Android 16 behavior changes"). Locking is therefore not a reliable guard on tablets and foldables.
  • Android 8.0 specific: a translucent/floating Activity that requested a fixed orientation crashed with IllegalStateException: Only fullscreen opaque activities can request orientation; fixed from 8.1.
  • Users who rotate to read in landscape with a locked app experience letterbox/compat mode.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity
    android:name=".CameraActivity"
    android:screenOrientation="portrait" />   <!-- or sensorPortrait/userPortrait -->
// Runtime, e.g. while recording
requestedOrientation = ActivityInfo.SCREEN_ORIENTATION_LOCKED

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Locking portrait to "fix" a video restart or dialog bug, then seeing the same bug from dark mode.
  • Locking in the manifest of a library Activity, forcing the host app's rotation.
  • Using SCREEN_ORIENTATION_LOCKED during a task and forgetting to restore it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. portrait vs sensorPortrait vs userPortrait? → portrait fixed upright; sensorPortrait allows 180 degree flip; userPortrait follows sensor but respects the user's auto-rotate toggle.
  2. How do you keep an app that is portrait-only on phones but responsive on tablets? → Set no manifest lock and lock at runtime only for compact width via WindowSizeClass.
  3. Does the lock apply in split-screen? → Often ignored in multi-window; you must not rely on it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Yes, lock to portrait". Senior: rotation lock is cosmetic, other triggers remain, tablets may ignore it, so state handling must be correct regardless.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app locked to portrait blamed "dark mode" tickets on OEM bugs for months; the real cause was unsaved state on any recreate.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a ViewModel survive rotation, and what exactly does it not survive?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common Android interview question. The senior signal is knowing the boundary: config change yes, process death and finish no.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A ViewModel lives in a ViewModelStore owned by the Activity; during a config change the store is handed to the next instance via onRetainNonConfigurationInstance, so I get the same ViewModel back. It is cleared only when the owner is truly finishing. It does not survive process death, finish()/back, or the user swiping the app away, so for restore I need SavedStateHandle or persistence.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity#1 ----> ViewModelStore {MainViewModel}
   | config change: onRetainNonConfigurationInstance() -> NonConfigurationInstances(viewModelStore)
Activity#2 <---- same store via getLastNonConfigurationInstance()

Back press / finish():   store.clear() -> ViewModel.onCleared()
Process death:           whole heap gone, store gone

ComponentActivity registers a lifecycle observer that, on ON_DESTROY, calls viewModelStore.clear() only if !isChangingConfigurations. Since the ViewModel outlives the Activity instance, it must never hold a View, Activity, Fragment, or anything with a Context of the Activity (AndroidViewModel gives the application context for that reason). It keeps running coroutines in viewModelScope across rotation, which is the reason network calls do not restart.

What it does not survive: process death (state in memory gone), finish(), task removal, and, importantly, a new ViewModel scope (e.g. a Navigation back stack entry that is popped).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SearchViewModel(private val handle: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {
    // survives process death too: small, serializable
    val query = handle.getStateFlow("q", "")
    // survives rotation only: large, re-derivable
    private val _results = MutableStateFlow<List<Item>>(emptyList())
    val results = _results.asStateFlow()
    fun setQuery(q: String) { handle["q"] = q }
}
// Activity
private val vm: SearchViewModel by viewModels()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing an Activity or View in the ViewModel (classic leak).
  • Assuming ViewModel data is there after process death.
  • Exposing mutable state and mutating it from the Activity.
  • Using activityViewModels() and being surprised the ViewModel lives until the Activity dies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is the ViewModelStore kept physically? → In ActivityClientRecord.lastNonConfigurationInstances in ActivityThread, via NonConfigurationInstances.
  2. Does a ViewModel survive a dark-mode change? → Yes, it is also a config change.
  3. What happens to viewModelScope jobs on rotation vs back? → Kept on rotation, cancelled in onCleared on finish.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "ViewModel survives rotation". Senior: describes the retain mechanism, isChangingConfigurations, the leak rules, and pairs it with SavedStateHandle for process death.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cart screen lost items after the user took a phone call for 20 minutes; the data sat only in the ViewModel and the process was killed behind the call app.

questions.promptHtml: What does android:configChanges do, and why do most style guides say not to use it to "fix" rotation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that it's an opt-out that shifts responsibility to you, and that it hides state bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It tells the system, "for these configuration fields, don't recreate me, call onConfigurationChanged instead". The Resources object is already updated, but I must re-apply layout, strings and drawables manually. It's valid for narrow cases (video player, game, a camera preview, multi-window apps that handle resize) but discouraged as a general fix: it doesn't prevent recreation for undeclared changes or process death, and it creates a second code path nobody tests.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• You declare a pipe-separated list; the system relaunches only if the changed bits are not in the declared set. See Q023 table.
  • The Activity instance persists, so Views are not re-inflated and layout-land is not applied automatically. You must reload anything configuration dependent in onConfigurationChanged.
  • Fragments in that Activity are not recreated either, and neither are dialogs; their state is fine, but their resources may be stale.
  • Android doc stance: use it as a last resort, mainly for performance-critical cases.
  • It does not apply to Application; the Application is always notified.
  • Locale-related caveat: declaring locale but not layoutDirection leaves the layout direction wrong for RTL languages. Declare both. Same for orientation + screenSize + smallestScreenSize + screenLayout.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity
    android:name=".PlayerActivity"
    android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize|smallestScreenSize|screenLayout|keyboardHidden" />
override fun onConfigurationChanged(newConfig: Configuration) {
    super.onConfigurationChanged(newConfig)
    // Resources are updated; re-bind whatever depends on orientation/size
    binding.controls.isVisible = newConfig.orientation == Configuration.ORIENTATION_LANDSCAPE
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding orientation alone on API 13+ (still recreated; need screenSize|smallestScreenSize).
  • Declaring uiMode and forgetting to refresh colors, so dark mode shows half old, half new UI.
  • Using it so that "state loss goes away" while process death still destroys everything.
  • Forgetting that AppCompatDelegate night mode relies on recreation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Application's onConfigurationChanged affected? → No, always called.
  2. How do Compose screens fare? → Compose recomposes with the new config via LocalConfiguration; handling config yourself is common in Compose-heavy single-Activity apps, still lose any View-based assets.
  3. Why did the docs add smallestScreenSize in API 13? → Because screen size (dp) now changes on rotation, not just orientation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it stops recreation on rotation, so we use it". Senior: describes the exact cost (manual resource refresh, still need persistence), the bits that must go together, and when it is legitimate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team added configChanges="orientation|screenSize" to every Activity to kill a rotation bug; split-screen resize and font-scale changes then displayed stale layouts for months.

questions.promptHtml: Who receives onConfigurationChanged, when, and what are the pitfalls of using it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know the Activity/Application/ComponentCallbacks split from those who only know the Activity callback.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Application, Services, ContentProviders and registered ComponentCallbacks get it for every configuration change, because they aren't recreated. An Activity gets it only for bits listed in configChanges; otherwise it is relaunched without that call. In the callback Resources is already updated, so I re-apply resource dependent UI and call super.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Application.onConfigurationChanged, Service.onConfigurationChanged, ContentProvider.onConfigurationChanged, Fragment.onConfigurationChanged (only when its Activity is not recreated) and anything registered via registerComponentCallbacks() receive the new Configuration.
  • The newConfig is the full snapshot; compare with the previous one if you care about a specific field (diff() returns a bitmask).
  • Not every config change reaches views: an Activity-level change delivers to the view tree through View.onConfigurationChanged, helpful for custom views that cache sizes.
  • Use registerComponentCallbacks in places like a media layer that needs fontScale/locale changes without holding an Activity.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        registerComponentCallbacks(object : ComponentCallbacks2 {
            override fun onConfigurationChanged(newConfig: Configuration) {
                Locale.setDefault(newConfig.locales[0]) // keep a cached formatter in sync
            }
            override fun onLowMemory() {}
            override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {}
        })
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not calling super.onConfigurationChanged.
  • Caching Resources strings/dimens in a singleton at startup, then never refreshing after locale change.
  • Reading resources.configuration from the Application context to decide dark mode: Application resources may not reflect an Activity-level uiMode override from AppCompatDelegate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does ContextThemeWrapper with overrideConfiguration receive it? → No, it only changes the wrapper's resources.
  2. Can a Fragment get onConfigurationChanged if its Activity is recreated? → No; the Fragment is recreated too.
  3. Which context do I use for localized strings in a singleton? → Application context only works for system locale; for per-app or overridden locale use the Activity (or recreate/refresh).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it's the callback when I handle rotation myself". Senior: lists all receivers, the full-Configuration semantics, and the singleton staleness trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Date formatting stayed in the old locale in a notification helper that cached a DateFormat in a singleton; fixed by invalidating it from an Application-level ComponentCallbacks.

questions.contextHtml: A video-course app (1.2M DAU, ~35% on 3-4 GB mid-range devices) plays 20-40 minute lessons. After a release, support reports "video restarts from 0 when I rotate" and watch-time per session drops 11%. Crashlytics is clean. The player is created in PlayerActivity.onCreate and released in onDestroy; last position is saved to the backend only every 30 s. The Activity has no configChanges. Logcat on rotation shows ExoPlayerImpl: Release ... then ExoPlayerImpl: Init ... within 150 ms. An engineer proposes configChanges="orientation|screenSize" plus screenOrientation="sensor".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose the bug and tell me how you'd fix it for good, including whether you'd accept the configChanges proposal.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add configChanges so the Activity isn't recreated." That hides the issue only for rotation. Dark mode, font scale or a multi-window resize still recreate, and the position is still lost on process death.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did it start with this release (what changed: player library bump, onDestroy release moved)? Is it all rotations or also dark mode toggles (tells me it's recreation, not rotation code)? Which players: Media3 ExoPlayer or MediaPlayer? Is playback expected to continue in background (PiP/audio)? How do we restore position on cold start?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that persists player.currentPosition and playWhenReady into onSaveInstanceState and restores them in onCreate; that is small and safe. Do not roll the whole feature back.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Player is bound to the Activity instance and rebuilt on recreation with no position carry-over, (b) a regression: previously position was stored in a ViewModel that someone removed, (c) buffering-time red herring: the 150 ms init gap, (d) analytics bug counting restarts, (e) a backend resume-point overwritten by the zero position posted from onDestroy.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with adb shell cmd uimode night yes (dark mode is a config change without rotating) and with rotation. Log isChangingConfigurations in onDestroy. Check the position upload path to see if a 0 is sent on destroy (hypothesis e). Diff the last release to see who removed the saved state.
  5. Root cause: The player instance is owned by the Activity, which is a throwaway object. onDestroy releases it, and nothing hands the position to the new instance. The position was only in memory fields.
  6. Fix: Short term: save/restore position, playWhenReady, mediaItemIndex via the Bundle. Long term: hold playback state in a ViewModel with SavedStateHandle; keep the ExoPlayer in a MediaSessionService/ViewModel (Media3 guidance) so rotation just re-attaches the surface.
class PlayerViewModel(private val h: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {
    var positionMs: Long
        get() = h["pos"] ?: 0L
        set(v) { h["pos"] = v }
    var playWhenReady: Boolean
        get() = h["play"] ?: true
        set(v) { h["play"] = v }
}
// Activity
override fun onStart() { super.onStart(); initPlayer() }
override fun onStop() {
    vm.positionMs = player.currentPosition
    vm.playWhenReady = player.playWhenReady
    player.release(); super.onStop()
}
private fun initPlayer() {
    player = ExoPlayer.Builder(this).build().also {
        it.setMediaItem(item); it.seekTo(vm.positionMs)
        it.playWhenReady = vm.playWhenReady; it.prepare()
        binding.playerView.player = it
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Instrumented test using ActivityScenario.recreate() with a fake player asserting position carry-over; a rule that anything the user would be annoyed to lose goes in the ViewModel/SavedStateHandle.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use configChanges as the main fix: it covers rotation only, and it can leave the surface/layout stale. I'd accept it as an additional optimisation for a pure fullscreen player screen once state is correct, since it avoids the visible black flash. I'd not keep the whole player in a static field either (leaks the surface).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rotation black flash remains after the fix; why? → Releasing and recreating the player and surface costs ~150-400 ms. Keep the player in a ViewModel/service and swap the surface, or handle config for that one screen.
  • What about a phone call killing the process mid-lesson? → SavedStateHandle covers it; also push position to backend every 10-30 s and on onStop.
  • Does onStop or onDestroy release fit multi-window? → onStop on API 24+, since the Activity may be visible but paused in multi-window.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a streaming app: the fix passed rotation tests but dark-mode auto-switch at 7 pm restarted episodes for hundreds of thousands of users. Recreation tests became part of every media PR.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests configChanges or portrait lock as the fix, no mention of other triggers or process death.
  • Hire: Persists position through ViewModel/Bundle, recognises dark mode as a trigger, can explain the release placement.
  • Strong hire: Separates state from the player object, discusses service-owned player, surface re-attach, backend resume-point race, and tests via recreate().

questions.promptHtml: What was setRetainInstance(true) for, why was it deprecated, and what do you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Legacy codebases still contain it; they want to see you can migrate it safely and explain why it was a bad abstraction.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A retained Fragment survives a config change: its instance and fields are reused, only its view is destroyed and re-created (onCreate/onDestroy are skipped). It was used to keep AsyncTasks, sockets and big objects across rotation. It was deprecated in AndroidX Fragment 1.3.0 because ViewModel does the same thing with a clearer lifecycle and without the sharp edges (hidden lifecycle, retained fragments with no UI, leaks when they hold Activity references). Replacement: ViewModel, plus SavedStateHandle for process death.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanically, retained fragments are stored in FragmentManagerViewModel (a ViewModel itself, in recent versions) via NonConfigurationInstances. A retained fragment:

  • skips onCreate/onDestroy on config change, but still goes through onAttach/onDetach and view callbacks,
  • cannot be retained if it lives in the back stack in older versions (retention only works for fragments not on the back stack), and cannot be nested within a non-retained parent (a child retained fragment needs a retained parent),
  • keeps references to any listener or Context you stored, which now point to a destroyed Activity.

Since Fragment 1.3.0 setRetainInstance is deprecated and the FragmentManager's own state is held in a ViewModel, so the Fragment API and the ViewModel API share one retention mechanism.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Migration:

// Before (deprecated)
class WorkerFragment : Fragment() {
    init { retainInstance = true }
    var task: Job? = null
}
// After
class WorkViewModel : ViewModel() {
    val state = MutableStateFlow<UiState>(UiState.Idle)
    fun start() = viewModelScope.launch { /* work */ }
}
class ScreenFragment : Fragment(R.layout.screen) {
    private val vm: WorkViewModel by viewModels()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Migrating the Fragment's fields into the ViewModel but still passing the Fragment/Activity into it as a callback.
  • Assuming retained = survives process death.
  • Retaining a Fragment that holds a View or binding.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not retain fragments for a UI-less worker? → That is exactly what ViewModel replaces; retained UI-less fragment leaks and obscures lifecycle.
  2. Does a retained fragment's onCreate run again after rotation? → No; that is the visible symptom that code in onCreate is no longer one-off per instance.
  3. How does the FragmentManager itself survive rotation? → Its state is saved in the Bundle (android:support:fragments) and a FragmentManagerViewModel holds non-config state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it keeps data on rotation, now use ViewModel". Senior: describes the lifecycle skip of onCreate/onDestroy, back stack and nesting restrictions, the common leak, and the migration path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A legacy checkout flow retained a worker fragment holding the old Activity as a listener; each rotation leaked a whole Activity until LeakCanary flagged the chain.

questions.contextHtml:
A support-ticket form (800k MAU, 4% on API 26-28) shows a bug: after rotation the "Subject" field is empty, the "Priority" spinner is reset, but the "Description" field survives. Product says it's inconsistent. The layout and Activity are below.

<LinearLayout ...>
  <EditText android:id="@+id/subject" ... />
  <Spinner  android:id="@+id/priority" ... />
  <com.acme.ui.NotesView android:id="@+id/notes" ... />   <!-- custom view -->
</LinearLayout>
class NotesView(c: Context, a: AttributeSet) : LinearLayout(c, a) {
    var text: String = ""
    // no onSaveInstanceState/onRestoreInstanceState
}
class FormActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(b)
        setContentView(R.layout.form)
        findViewById<EditText>(R.id.subject).setText(viewModel.draft.subject) // always
        findViewById<Spinner>(R.id.priority).adapter = adapter               // new adapter every time
    }
}

The Description field is a plain EditText inside NotesView. Logs are clean; the issue reproduces in dark mode toggle too.
questions.promptHtml: Explain every symptom, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use onSaveInstanceState to save each field by hand." That works but misses why one field survives and others don't, and ignores that the system already handles the standard views.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the Subject EditText have an android:id in all layout variants? Is the ViewModel's draft updated as the user types, or only on submit? Is android:saveEnabled="false" set anywhere? Is it the same on API 28 and 33?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I'd treat it as a bug fix this sprint. If the form is business-critical I'd stop overwriting the field in onCreate first, which is a one-line change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Subject: restore failed, most likely a duplicate id (view state is keyed by id), or the id is missing in one layout variant. Note onRestoreInstanceState runs after onCreate, so a restored value would override the setText in onCreate; an empty field means nothing was restored, or the ViewModel draft is also empty. (b) Spinner: selection restored by position, but the adapter set after restore with different data wipes the selection. (c) NotesView: custom view saves child state by id; NotesView.text is a field not saved. (d) Red herring: the spinner placed in a RecyclerView.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a breakpoint on onRestoreInstanceState, dump the Bundle (android:viewHierarchyState sparse array) with Bundle.keySet(), check lint for "MissingId" and duplicate ids (DuplicateIds lint). Toggle adb shell cmd uimode night yes for repro.
  5. Root cause: The platform restores view state only for views with unique ids in the hierarchy via SparseArray<Parcelable>, called during onRestoreInstanceState. Subject: duplicate id subject in an included layout makes two views write to the same key; the last one wins. Spinner: assigning the adapter after onRestoreInstanceState is irrelevant, but resetting the adapter with new items on each creation resets the selected position. NotesView: its children's ids (EditText) are saved, but the inner field text is not, and the view may have been inflated twice with the same ids.
  6. Fix: Unique ids, set adapter once in onCreate, keep drafts in a ViewModel updated on each text change, and give the custom view real state saving.
class NotesView(c: Context, a: AttributeSet) : LinearLayout(c, a) {
    var text = ""
    override fun onSaveInstanceState(): Parcelable =
        Bundle().apply {
            putParcelable("super", super.onSaveInstanceState())
            putString("text", text)
        }
    override fun onRestoreInstanceState(state: Parcelable?) {
        val b = state as? Bundle ?: return super.onRestoreInstanceState(state)
        text = b.getString("text", "")
        super.onRestoreInstanceState(b.getParcelable("super")) // API 33+: use getParcelable(key, Class)
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Lint DuplicateIds; test ActivityScenario.recreate() on every form; one-line review rule: "every stateful view needs an id and either platform restore or a ViewModel".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't hand-save each field in onSaveInstanceState (duplicates what the framework does). I wouldn't set saveEnabled=false to dodge conflicts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two instances of the same layout on screen with the same ids? → They overwrite each other's state; use android:saveEnabled per instance with a unique tag or manual state.
  • Why does RecyclerView item text vanish after rotation? → RecyclerView doesn't save item views' state; bind from your model.
  • Does Compose do this automatically? → No; rememberSaveable is required (A3).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A bank form kept dropping the "amount" field only on tablets. Two included layout variants shared one id and one included a hidden duplicate; the fix was a 2-line id rename.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Manually saves every field in the Bundle without understanding why some fields survive.
  • Hire: Explains id-based hierarchy restore, duplicate ids, adapter reset, custom view state.
  • Strong hire: Adds BaseSavedState/Bundle approach, ordering of onRestoreInstanceState, lint, and test via recreate().
